question.prompt: Why might the proposed walking loop need adjustment?

options.text: the football goals are already permanent
people waiting for friends sometimes stand in its path

question.explanation: The observers record standing pupils in the proposed route. That observation suggests a practical conflict to test rather than proof that walking is impossible.

stimulus.title: Who uses the oval?
stimulus.body:
Two suggestions reached the school council about the oval. One group wanted permanent football goals. Another wanted a marked walking loop. The council asked pupils to observe how the oval was used at three different times each day for a week.

At lunch, football players occupied most of the centre. Before school, smaller groups walked around the edge. After school, the oval was often empty, though on two afternoons a sports club trained there. The observers noted that pupils waiting for friends sometimes stood where a proposed walking loop would run.

The council rejected the idea that the most visible activity must be the only important one. It recommended movable goals and a trial walking route marked with cones. This would preserve options while revealing whether the activities interfered with each other. The recommendation did not give every group everything it wanted. It gave the school a way to learn before fixing equipment permanently in place.

workedSolution: The observers record standing pupils in the proposed route.
That observation suggests a practical conflict to test rather than proof that walking is impossible.

question.prompt: Why does Daniel first open the window?

options.text: the room is hot and stuffy

question.explanation: The first paragraph describes the hottest day and a stuffy room. His initial opening is for comfort, not a deliberate attempt to perform publicly.

stimulus.title: An open window
stimulus.body:
Every afternoon, Daniel practised his clarinet with the window closed. He imagined the whole street waiting for his mistakes. On the hottest day of term, the room grew so stuffy that he pushed the window open before beginning.

Halfway through a scale, he missed a note and stopped. From the garden next door came a voice: 'Was that the end?'

Daniel lowered the instrument. 'It was supposed to keep going.'

'Then I shall wait,' said the neighbour.

He began again, more quietly. This time he reached the top of the scale. The neighbour did not clap or offer a lesson. She simply resumed watering her tomatoes.

The next afternoon the weather was cooler. Daniel closed the window out of habit, then opened it a little. He still chose a time when few people were outside, and he still disliked the squeak near the end of the piece. But when it came, he played the next note instead of putting the clarinet away.

workedSolution: The first paragraph describes the hottest day and a stuffy room.
His initial opening is for comfort, not a deliberate attempt to perform publicly.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

stimulus.title: An open window
stimulus.body:
Every afternoon, Daniel practised his clarinet with the window closed. He imagined the whole street waiting for his mistakes. On the hottest day of term, the room grew so stuffy that he pushed the window open before beginning.

Halfway through a scale, he missed a note and stopped. From the garden next door came a voice: 'Was that the end?'

Daniel lowered the instrument. 'It was supposed to keep going.'

'Then I shall wait,' said the neighbour.

He began again, more quietly. This time he reached the top of the scale. The neighbour did not clap or offer a lesson. She simply resumed watering her tomatoes.

The next afternoon the weather was cooler. Daniel closed the window out of habit, then opened it a little. He still chose a time when few people were outside, and he still disliked the squeak near the end of the piece. But when it came, he played the next note instead of putting the clarinet away.

workedSolution: He chooses a quieter time and still dislikes errors, showing lingering self-consciousness.
Opening the window and continuing nevertheless show a measured increase in willingness.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

stimulus.title: A fictional sound experiment
stimulus.body:
In a classroom model, three groups investigated how the length of a stretched elastic band related to its sound. They used bands of the same kind and plucked them over identical empty boxes. Each group shortened its band gradually and described the pitch it heard.

All three groups reported higher pitches at shorter lengths. However, the bands were stretched by hand. One group pulled much harder than another, and none measured tension. Their descriptions of pitch were also based on listening rather than a recording device.

The class wrote a cautious conclusion: 'Under our test conditions, shorter lengths were associated with higher perceived pitch.' They did not write that length alone had been proved to cause every change. For a new trial, they planned a frame that could hold tension more consistently. They would keep the boxes and band material the same. Their aim was to reduce one uncertainty at a time, not to pretend the first trial had taught them nothing.

workedSolution: The second paragraph directly reports higher pitches at shorter lengths.
Tension was not measured, so that cannot be part of the established observation.

question.prompt: Describe the same market stall twice: once through the eyes of an excited visitor and once through the eyes of the tired stallholder. Keep the physical objects consistent. Allow 15 minutes in total, including any planning and editing you choose to do.

question.explanation: List a few fixed objects, then decide which each observer would value or resent. Change focus, comparisons and rhythm to express viewpoint while preserving those shared objects.
